board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1

lessons.unit: Unit 1: South America and the Amazon
lessons.title: Locating South America: countries and landscapes
objectives: Locate South America and name some of its countries
Identify the Andes, the Amazon River and the Atacama Desert
Describe the main physical features of the continent

keywords.def: a continent in the southern and western hemispheres, between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans
the longest mountain range on land, along the west of South America
the river that carries the most water of any river on Earth
a place that gets very little rainfall
a natural part of the landscape, like a mountain or river

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the seven continents.
Which line around the Earth separates the northern and southern hemispheres?

teach.heading: Where is South America?
bullets: South America is a continent in the western half of the world.
The Pacific Ocean lies to the west. The Atlantic lies to the east.
The Equator crosses the north of the continent.
teach.note: Show a world map and ask children to find South America. Point out that the Equator passes through Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil. Many children confuse South America with Africa because the coastlines look similar. Ask them to trace the outline of each.

teach.heading: Countries of South America
bullets: There are twelve independent countries.
Brazil is the largest. Others: Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia.
Most people speak Spanish. In Brazil they speak Portuguese.
teach.note: Display a political map and read the countries together: Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Uruguay, Venezuela, Guyana and Suriname. French Guiana is a French territory, not a country. Ask why Brazil speaks Portuguese: Portugal once ruled the area.

teach.heading: The Andes mountains
bullets: The Andes run down the west coast for about 7,000 km.
They are the longest mountain range on Earth.
Aconcagua in Argentina is 6,961 m high.
teach.note: Compare the Andes with the UK's highest mountain, Ben Nevis at 1,345 m. Aconcagua is about five times as high. Mention that the Andes have formed where tectonic plates collide, linking to earlier work on volcanoes and earthquakes.

teach.heading: Rivers and deserts
bullets: The Amazon River flows from the Andes across Brazil to the Atlantic.
The Amazon carries more water than any other river.
The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places.
teach.note: Show a satellite image of the Amazon River mouth. The Amazon holds about one-fifth of all the river water that flows into the oceans. The Atacama is on the west side of the Andes, so mountains block the rain. Ask children how the same continent can have both the biggest river and a very dry desert.

practice: Label five countries on a blank map of South America.
Mark and name the Andes, the Amazon River and the Atacama Desert.
independent: Create a labelled map of South America with ten labels.
Write five sentences describing the physical geography of the continent.
Stretch: explain why the Andes affect the climate on either side.
exit: Name two countries in South America.
What is the longest mountain range in the world?
lessons.homework: Use an atlas or online map to find the capital cities of five South American countries and list them.
lessons.send: Provide a labelled map for support. EAL: pre-teach country names with flags. Stretch: ask pupils to compare South America with Africa in terms of size and features.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: South America and the Amazon
lessons.title: Brazil: people, cities and culture
objectives: Locate Brazil and its main cities
Describe where people live and why
Compare life in Brazil with life in the UK

keywords.def: the city where a country's government is based
the number of people living in a place
the land beside the sea
the way of life, food, clothing, language and beliefs of a group of people

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the longest mountain range on Earth.
Name three countries in South America.
What is the Amazon River famous for?

teach.heading: Brazil: a giant country
bullets: Brazil is the biggest country in South America.
It covers almost half the continent.
Over 200 million people live there.
teach.note: Show a map highlighting Brazil. It is the fifth largest country in the world by area and by population. Compare with the UK: Brazil is about 35 times larger than the UK. Ask children what challenges a very big country might have.

teach.heading: Cities of Brazil
bullets: The capital city is Brasilia.
The biggest city is Sao Paulo. Rio de Janeiro is famous for its beaches.
Most Brazilians live near the east coast.
teach.note: Locate the three cities on a map. Brasilia was built in the 1950s and became the capital in 1960, to encourage people to move inland. Ask children why most people live near the coast: ports, trade, warmer climate, history. Rio's Christ the Redeemer statue is a well-known landmark.

teach.heading: Life and culture
bullets: Brazilians speak Portuguese.
Football, food and family life are big parts of the culture.
People come from many backgrounds, including Indigenous, African, European and Arab.
teach.note: Share photographs of food (rice and beans, cassava), football and the Amazon. Mention that Brazil has one of the largest populations of people with Arab (especially Lebanese and Syrian) heritage outside the Arab world, and a Muslim community. Keep the focus on respect for different cultures.

teach.heading: Rich and poor in Brazil
bullets: Some parts of Brazilian cities are wealthy.
Many people live in favelas, which are crowded neighbourhoods.
Many favela residents build their own homes.
teach.note: Show photographs sensitively. Avoid stereotypes: favelas are communities with schools, shops and strong community bonds, even though they often lack services like sewers or reliable electricity. Ask what the government could do to help improve life there.

practice: Find and label Brazil's three biggest cities on a map.
Write two ways life in Brazil is similar to the UK and two ways it is different.
independent: Make a Brazil fact file: capital, language, population, cities, landmarks.
Draw a Venn diagram comparing life in Brazil and the UK.
Stretch: explain why more people live near the coast than inland.
exit: What is the capital of Brazil?
What language do most Brazilians speak?
lessons.homework: Research one famous Brazilian food, sport or festival and write three sentences.
lessons.send: Provide a fact-file template with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach city names and use maps. Stretch: use population data to calculate how many times bigger Brazil is than the UK.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: South America and the Amazon
lessons.title: The Amazon rainforest: layers and life
objectives: Describe the climate of the Amazon rainforest
Name and describe the four layers of the rainforest
Explain how plants and animals are adapted to rainforest life

keywords.def: a thick forest in a hot, wet part of the world
the thick layer of leaves and branches high above the ground
the tallest trees that rise above the canopy
the dark, shady layer beneath the canopy
the variety of living things in a place

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the capital of Brazil?
Which river runs through the Amazon rainforest?
Is a rainforest hot or cold? Wet or dry? Why do you think so?

teach.heading: The Amazon rainforest
bullets: The Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world.
It is shared by nine countries. About 60% is in Brazil.
It is hot and wet all year round.
teach.note: Show a map of the Amazon basin. The rainforest is near the Equator, which is why it is hot (25 to 27 degrees Celsius) and receives more than 2,000 mm of rain a year (the UK gets around 1,000 mm). Ask children to describe what it would feel like to stand there.

teach.heading: Four layers
bullets: Emergent layer: the tallest trees, over 45 m.
Canopy: thick roof of leaves, 30 to 45 m up.
Understorey and forest floor: dark, damp and quiet.
teach.note: Use a labelled cross-section. Ask which layer gets the most light (emergent and canopy) and which gets the least (forest floor, about 2% of sunlight). Link to adaptation: plants in the understorey have big leaves to catch light.

teach.heading: Life in the rainforest
bullets: The Amazon is home to about 10% of known species.
Jaguars, sloths, macaws and piranhas live here.
Animals are adapted to their layer, like a sloth in the trees.
teach.note: Show photographs of animals in their layers. Point out adaptations such as a toucan's large bill for reaching fruit on thin branches or a sloth's slow metabolism and long claws. Note the word biodiversity and ask why many species can live together.

teach.heading: People of the forest
bullets: Hundreds of Indigenous groups live in the Amazon.
They use the forest for food, medicine and homes.
Their knowledge helps protect the forest.
teach.note: Show a respectful photograph or video. Explain that Indigenous peoples have lived in the Amazon for thousands of years and use plants for food and medicines without destroying the forest. Ask why we should listen to them when making decisions.

practice: Label the four layers on a rainforest cross-section.
Match animals to the layer where they live, and say why.
independent: Draw and label a rainforest cross-section showing all four layers and two animals in each.
Write a paragraph beginning: 'The Amazon rainforest is hot and wet because ...'
Stretch: choose one animal and explain how it is adapted to its layer.
exit: Name two layers of the rainforest.
Why is the rainforest hot and wet?
lessons.homework: Research one rainforest animal and draw it in its layer, with a sentence about how it survives.
lessons.send: Provide a diagram with layer names to match. EAL: use pictures for animals and layers. Stretch: compare the Amazon with a temperate forest in the UK.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: South America and the Amazon
lessons.title: Deforestation: why the Amazon is in danger
objectives: Explain what deforestation is and why it happens
Suggest ways to protect the rainforest

keywords.def: cutting down or burning large areas of forest
farming cows for meat on large areas of land
using resources in a way that will not run out or harm the future
the natural home of a plant or animal

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four layers of the rainforest.
Why is the Amazon rainforest important to the world?

teach.heading: What is deforestation?
bullets: Deforestation is clearing forest for other uses.
Large areas of the Amazon have been cleared.
Much of the clearing happens in Brazil.
teach.note: Show satellite pictures of the same part of the Amazon from different years. Ask children what changed. About one sixth of the Amazon rainforest has been lost in the last fifty years. Avoid saying 'the lungs of the Earth': the rainforest absorbs a lot of carbon dioxide but also uses much of the oxygen it makes.

teach.heading: Why is it cleared?
bullets: Cattle ranching is the main cause.
Farmers grow soya beans for animal feed.
Logging, mining and new roads also clear forest.
teach.note: Link to everyday life: soya and beef are sold around the world. Ask where the food we eat comes from. Be fair: people clearing the forest are often poor farmers trying to make a living, as well as big companies. Ask children to suggest what might help both people and the forest.

teach.heading: What are the effects?
bullets: Animals lose their habitat and some may die out.
Soil washes away without tree roots.
Burning trees adds carbon dioxide to the air.
teach.note: Use a simple chain of cause and effect: trees cut, roots gone, rain washes soil, rivers muddy. Connect to climate change: trees store carbon, so when they burn, the carbon dioxide goes into the air. Indigenous peoples also lose their homes.

teach.heading: Protecting the rainforest
bullets: Create protected parks and reserves.
Choose sustainable wood and farming.
Allah made us stewards of the Earth (Qur'an 2:30).
teach.note: Qur'an 2:30 tells that Allah is placing a khalifah on the Earth. Explain the idea of khalifah as caretaker. Ask children what they can do: reduce waste, support sustainable products, learn and tell others. Note that governments, companies and communities all have a part.

practice: Make a cause and effect chain for deforestation with at least four links.
Discuss: What would you say to a farmer who wants to clear forest? What could you offer instead?
independent: Write a letter to the president of Brazil explaining why the rainforest matters.
Make a poster with three ways to protect the Amazon.
Stretch: explain why protecting the forest can help people on the other side of the world.
exit: Give one cause and one effect of deforestation.
lessons.homework: Look at the labels of two products at home and find out if they contain palm oil, soya or beef. Write what you found.
lessons.send: Provide a cause-and-effect template. EAL: pre-teach deforestation with images. Stretch: debate whether it is fair to ask poorer countries to protect forests for the world.

lessons.title: What is an island?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is Great Britain an island, and does it matter?
objectives: To understand what an island is and locate important islands on a world map
successCriteria: All: say what an island is
Most: locate five islands and island countries on a world map
Some: compare the size of different islands

keywords.def: land with water all around it
one of seven very large areas of land
a group of islands
where the land meets the sea
a country made up of one or more islands

hook.text: Imagine you live on a small island. What would be easy and what would be hard?

islamicLink.text: The Muslim geographer al-Idrisi (born about 1100) made a famous world map in Sicily in 1154 for the island's king, Roger II. Allah says He placed the stars so people could find their way across land and sea (al-An'am 6:97). Muslims have long studied maps and the sea to travel, trade and learn.

starter.q: Name the ocean to the west of the UK.

teach.heading: What is an island?
bullets: Land with water all around
Smaller than a continent
Can be tiny or huge
teach.note: Ask: is Australia an island? It is usually counted as a continent, so Greenland is the largest island.

teach.heading: Great Britain is an island
bullets: England, Scotland and Wales share it
The UK also includes Northern Ireland
Plus many smaller islands
teach.note: Show the British Isles: Great Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man, the Hebrides, Orkney, Shetland.

teach.heading: Islands of the world
bullets: Some islands are huge
teach.note: Sizes rounded.

teach.heading: Island countries
bullets: Indonesia: over 17,000 islands
Maldives: about 1,200 islands
Iceland, Sri Lanka, Bahrain, Japan
teach.note: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country. The Maldives is an archipelago in the Indian Ocean.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
check.why: Greenland is the largest island; Great Britain is ninth.

practice.q: Is Sicily an island? How do you know?
practice.a: Yes: it has sea all around it
practice.model:
Look at Sicily on the map.
Trace the coast all the way round.
Water on every side, so it is an island.

independent.q: Core: On a world map, mark and label Greenland, Great Britain, Madagascar, Sicily, Sri Lanka and the Maldives.
independent.a: Greenland north-east of Canada; Great Britain north-west Europe; Madagascar off south-east Africa; Sicily south of Italy; Sri Lanka south of India; Maldives south-west of India
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: find India, look south, the tear-shaped island is Sri Lanka; label it.

independent.q: Extend: Label the ocean or sea around each island.
independent.a: Greenland: Arctic and Atlantic; Great Britain: Atlantic and North Sea; Madagascar and Maldives and Sri Lanka: Indian; Sicily: Mediterranean

independent.q: Stretch: Give one advantage and one challenge of living on an island.
independent.a: For example: fishing and trade by sea; harder to travel and get goods

exit.q: Big question: is Great Britain an island, and does it matter?
exit.a: Yes; it matters because the sea affected its trade, defence, weather and history

lessons.homework: Find three islands on a map or globe at home and list which ocean each is in.
lessons.send: SEND: map with islands pre-dotted and a word bank. EAL: island, sea, coast with pictures. Stretch: find the world's second-largest island (New Guinea).

lessons.title: Compass points and four-figure grid references
lessons.bigQuestion: How can two numbers tell you exactly where the treasure is?
objectives: To understand how to use compass directions and four-figure grid references on a map
successCriteria: All: use the eight compass points
Most: give a four-figure grid reference for a square
Some: give directions between two places using compass points and grid references

keywords.def: a tool that shows north, south, east and west
numbers that show a square on a map
a line going up the map; read along first
a line going across the map; read up second
between north and east

hook.text: How would you tell a friend on the phone exactly where something is on a map?

islamicLink.text: Muslims need directions every day: we face the qiblah, towards the Ka'bah in Makkah, when we pray. Allah says: turn your face towards al-Masjid al-Haram (al-Baqarah 2:144). Muslim scientists made instruments and maps to find the qiblah accurately.

starter.q: Name the four main compass points.

teach.heading: Eight compass points
bullets: N, E, S, W
NE, SE, SW, NW
'Naughty Elephants Squirt Water'
teach.note: Clockwise from north. The in-between points join two names, north or south always first.

teach.heading: Barakah Island map
bullets: Our own practice map
Columns: eastings
Rows: northings
teach.note: Read the square by its bottom-left corner: along the corridor, then up the stairs.

teach.heading: Along the corridor, up the stairs
bullets: Read along first: easting
Then up: northing
Village: 0203
teach.note: Model: the village is in column 02, row 03, so 0203.

model.problem: Give the grid reference of the lake.

teach.heading: Giving directions
bullets: The lighthouse is south of the river
The tor is north-west of the lake
teach.note: Use the map: from the lake, the tor is up and to the left: north-west.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which square is the harbour in?
check.why: Along first: column 04, then up: row 02, so 0402. Swapping them is the most common mistake.

practice.q: Give the grid reference of the farm.
practice.model:
Find the farm.
Along: column 02.
Up: row 02.
So 0202.

practice.q: Which direction is the cliffs from the village?

independent.q: Core: Give the four-figure grid reference for the beach, forest, river and tor.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: beach: along 01, up 03, so 0103.

independent.q: Extend: Which feature is south-east of the village?
Stretch: Write directions from the harbour to the tor using compass points and grid references.
independent.a: For example: from the harbour in 0402 go west to the farm in 0202, then north past the village in 0203 to the tor in 0204

exit.q: Big question: how can two numbers tell you exactly where the treasure is?
exit.a: The first gives the column (along) and the second the row (up), which together name one square

lessons.homework: Draw a grid over a sketch map of your bedroom and give grid references for three objects.
lessons.send: SEND: grid with columns and rows coloured; arrow showing 'along then up'. EAL: along, up, north, south. Stretch: hide a 'treasure' and write grid clues for a partner.

lessons.title: Latitude and longitude: finding islands anywhere
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you find any island on Earth with just two numbers?
objectives: To understand how latitude and longitude locate places on the globe
successCriteria: All: find the Equator and the Prime Meridian
Most: say whether a place is north or south, east or west
Some: locate an island from its latitude and longitude
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Muslim scholars in the history of geography

keywords.def: lines going around the globe, measured north or south of the Equator
lines from pole to pole, measured east or west of Greenwich
0° latitude
0° longitude, through Greenwich in London
a unit for measuring angles, written °

hook.text: A ship is lost at sea. What two pieces of information would help a rescuer find it?

islamicLink.text: Muslim astronomers worked out the latitude and longitude of many cities to find the qiblah and prayer times. Al-Khwarizmi, who worked in Baghdad in the 800s, made a list of places with their latitudes and longitudes. Allah says the sun and moon run by precise calculation (ar-Rahman 55:5).

starter.q: Village in square 0203. Which number is the easting?
What is between north and east?

teach.heading: Latitude
bullets: Lines go across, like a ladder
Equator is 0°
North Pole 90°N, South Pole 90°S
teach.note: Latitude, think 'ladder'. The UK is about 50° to 60° north.

teach.heading: Longitude
bullets: Lines go from pole to pole
Prime Meridian is 0°
Up to 180° east or west
teach.note: The Prime Meridian runs through Greenwich in London.

teach.heading: Islands by number
bullets: Rounded positions
teach.note: Find each on the globe as a class.

teach.heading: Reading a position
bullets: Latitude first, then longitude
Say N or S, then E or W
teach.note: Model: Madagascar 19°S, 47°E: south of the Equator, east of Greenwich.

steps: Look in the Mediterranean, south of Italy

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Madagascar is at about 19°S. It is:
check.why: S means south of the Equator.

practice.q: Is Iceland north or south of the Equator?
practice.model:
Look at the letter: N.
N means north.
Iceland is north of the Equator.

practice.q: Is Sri Lanka east or west of Greenwich?
What is the latitude of the Equator?

independent.q: Core: Find and label these on a world map: 54°N 2°W, 65°N 18°W, 19°S 47°E, 8°N 81°E.
independent.a: Great Britain, Iceland, Madagascar, Sri Lanka
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 54°N is well north; 2°W is just west of Greenwich: that is Great Britain.

independent.q: Extend: Which island is closest to the Equator: Sri Lanka, Sicily or Iceland?
Stretch: Bahrain is at about 26°N, 50°E. Describe where it is.
independent.a: North of the Equator and east of Greenwich, in the Persian Gulf, near Saudi Arabia

exit.q: Big question: how can you find any island on Earth with just two numbers?
exit.a: Latitude says how far north or south, longitude how far east or west; together they pinpoint it

lessons.homework: Find the latitude and longitude of your home town using an online map.
lessons.send: SEND: globe with the Equator and Prime Meridian coloured. EAL: north, south, east, west, degree. Stretch: find the latitude and longitude of Makkah (about 21°N, 40°E).

lessons.title: Symbols, keys and scale: reading the island
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a map be small but show a whole island?
objectives: To understand how symbols, keys and scale help us read a map
successCriteria: All: use a key to name map symbols
Most: use a scale to work out a distance
Some: describe the island's physical features using the map
lessons.smsc: Moral: accuracy and honesty in what we show others

keywords.def: a small picture or shape that stands for something
the list that explains the symbols
shows how distances on the map match real distances
a pile of rock on top of a hill
a natural feature like a hill, river or beach

hook.text: Why don't maps use photographs instead of symbols?

islamicLink.text: A map is honest only if its scale and key are true. Islam teaches truthfulness in everything: Allah says, 'O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words of truth' (al-Ahzab 33:70). Good map-makers show the land as it really is.

starter.q: Read a four-figure grid reference: along first, then ...

teach.heading: Symbols and the key
bullets: Symbols are simple and clear
The key explains them
Colours show features too
teach.note: Show an OS map key: church, campsite, footpath, viewpoint.

teach.heading: Our island key
bullets: Match each symbol
teach.note: Pupils match letters to numbers.

teach.heading: Scale
bullets: 1 cm on the map = 1 km on the ground
Measure with a ruler
Multiply by the scale
teach.note: Model: village to lighthouse measures 4 cm, so 4 km.

model.problem: Scale 1 cm = 1 km. Two places are 6 cm apart on the map. How far in real life?

teach.heading: What is a tor?
bullets: Bare rock on a hilltop
Made as softer rock wore away
Many on Dartmoor
teach.note: Show a photo of a tor on Dartmoor.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Scale 1 cm = 2 km. A path is 3 cm long on the map. Real length?
check.why: 3 x 2 = 6 km. Adding (5) or ignoring the scale (3) are the traps.

practice.q: Scale 1 cm = 1 km. The beach is 5 cm from the harbour. How far?
practice.model:
5 cm on the map.
1 cm = 1 km.
5 x 1 = 5 km.

practice.q: Is a lighthouse a physical or human feature?
Scale 1 cm = 2 km. 4 cm on the map is how far?

independent.q: Core: Draw a key for Barakah Island with a symbol for each of eight features.
independent.a: Eight clear symbols, each named in the key
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: triangle for the tor, blue oval for the lake, small tower for the lighthouse, each written in the key.

independent.q: Extend: Scale 1 cm = 2 km. The farm is 3.5 cm from the lighthouse. How far is that?
Stretch: Describe the physical features of the island in two sentences.
independent.a: For example: A rocky tor rises in the north, with forest beside it. A river runs south from the lake to the sea.

exit.q: Big question: why can a map be small but show a whole island?
exit.a: It uses a scale to shrink distances and symbols to show features simply

lessons.homework: Look at an online map of your area and find three symbols; write what each means.
lessons.send: SEND: symbol cards to match to the key. EAL: symbol, key, scale, distance. Stretch: draw a scale bar for your map.

lessons.title: Design your own island map
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes a map easy for someone else to use?
objectives: To understand how to combine grid, key, compass and scale to make a clear map
successCriteria: All: draw an island with a grid and a key
Most: add a compass and a scale
Some: write grid reference questions that work on your map
lessons.smsc: Social: peer checking with kind feedback

keywords.def: plan and make carefully
squares drawn over a map
explains the symbols
shows how map distances match real ones
shows the directions on a map

hook.text: If someone found your island map in a bottle, what would they need on it to find their way?

starter.q: Scale 1 cm = 1 km. 7 cm on the map is:
Write the grid reference: column 03, row 01.

teach.heading: A good map has
bullets: Title
Grid with numbers
Key
Compass rose
Scale
teach.note: Mnemonic: TGKCS or 'The Great Key Can Scale'.

teach.heading: Planning your island
bullets: Draw the coast first
Add 4 physical features
Add 4 human features
teach.note: Model on a 4 by 4 grid, numbered 01 to 04 along and up.

teach.heading: Check your map
bullets: Can a partner find each feature?
Is the key complete?
Is the scale clear?
teach.note: Peer check in breakout pairs with the checklist.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which is missing from this map: title, grid, key, scale?
check.why: The five essentials are title, grid, key, compass rose and scale.

practice.q: Write a grid reference question for Barakah Island.
practice.a: For example: What is in square 0303? (the lake)
practice.model:
Choose a feature: the lake.
